title: The banyan seed
hookLine: a father asks his son to break open a seed, and asks what he sees inside
carry: one unseen reality in everything, and you are that
tomorrow: karma: a ghost who needs work, and a dog's curly tail
last: EMPTY OF EGO, SO GOD CAN PLAY.

cards: Somewhere near you there's a very big tree. An oak, a maple, or, in India, a banyan, with roots dropping from its branches like ropes, wide enough to shade a whole village meeting.
That tree came from a seed smaller than a grain of rice. That part is common knowledge. But what's actually inside the seed?
A father in the Upanishads asks his son to look.

teach.h: BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.
teach.b: We're back in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, where Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu with things from around the house. Last week, it was salt in water. This time: bring me a fruit from that banyan tree.
Here it is, sir. Break it open. It's broken.
What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of those.
It's broken. What do you see there?

teach.h: FROM THAT, THE GREAT TREE STANDS.
teach.b: And the father says: this finest essence, the one you can't see, from that very thing this great banyan tree stands. Believe it, my dear. Then the refrain: that finest essence is the Self of all this.
That is the real. Tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu.
When Shvetaketu says nothing, he isn't wrong. He really can't see anything. But the tree is standing right there.
This is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas.
Brahman, the one reality, is in everything the way that essence is in the seed: unseen, and holding up the whole tree.
And that same essence is your own deepest self, the atman. You are that.
On the jnana road, knowledge doesn't mean collecting more facts; Shvetaketu already had twelve years of those. It means recognizing what can't be pointed at. And it changes how you see people.
Many teachers read the folded hands of namaste this way: a bow to the divine in the other person. The coworker, the stranger on the bus, the friend who annoys you: each one, a banyan seed.

how: The banyan seed teaching of the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta classes, sometimes with an actual fruit broken open, and the banyan tree itself is honored in many Hindu villages and temples.

o: action, even breaking a seed to look inside
the name of the banyan tree in Sanskrit
fate already written inside every seed

games.q: the banyan seed — tap the pairs.
p: from it, the great tree stands

s: Shvetaketu sees a tiny tree inside the seed
he sees nothing at all. the father's point is that the unseen essence is real.
this lesson ends with 'tat tvam asi'
the same refrain as the salt lesson: you are that, Shvetaketu.
the Upanishad says the unseen essence is in the tree but not in people
the same essence is the Self of all, and of Shvetaketu: tat tvam asi, you are that.

games.q: you're Shvetaketu. you've broken open a banyan seed and see nothing inside. what does your father say?
o: then there's nothing there: trust your eyes.
from that finest essence, the great tree stands. believe it.
games.why: the unseen essence is the root of the whole tree, and of everything: that is the Self, and you are that.

practice: Imagine a single seed in your palm, so small you could lose it, then picture the whole tree that could come from it: trunk, branches, a thousand leaves moving in the wind.
Turn the picture gently toward yourself and ask what's the finest thing in you, too fine to see; don't try to find it, just rest with the question, the way Shvetaketu stared at the broken seed.
If you pray, you can offer the question.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road today, the action is small: break the seed, look, and trust what you can't see.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the banyan tree, the word used in Chandogya 6.12; literally 'growing downward', for its hanging roots.

carryVoice: Your line: one unseen reality in everything, and you are that. Nothing at all, and a whole banyan. See you tomorrow.
